episodes.title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
episodes.description:
A single internal app now handles Railway's marketing content, email, social posts, media, creator relationships and launch planning. Mahmoud Abdelwahab built it with coding agents, but getting the features to run was only the beginning. The difference between a quick SaaS replacement and a tool his team wants to open every day lives in the details: background saving, responsive interactions, reversible actions and consistent screens. His starting point is a structured codebase with reusable abstractions, so each new feature follows existing patterns instead of inventing another way to do the same work.

Abdelwahab works through the product behaviors he has learned to request explicitly. Autosave should preserve progress without blocking typing; optimistic updates should make suitable actions feel immediate and recover when the operation fails. Undo and archiving give people room to change their minds. URL state makes a filtered view shareable, while infinite scrolling removes repetitive navigation. Referencing an existing page helps the agent reuse the app's interface and data fetching conventions. He then packages recurring design and deployment preferences into agent skills. The final step is a verification loop that opens the running application and exercises the feature from start to finish, because a successful build and passing tests can still leave a broken experience. These are practical lessons from an internal tool, without a claim of measured financial savings.

episodes.title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model — Branislav Brzak, Stealthium
episodes.description:
Three microseconds of extra latency can reveal activity on another tenant's GPU slice. Branislav Brzak demonstrates an H100 timing side channel that probes only the attacker's own memory, without reading the victim's memory or exploiting a software bug. His experiments use the signal to infer model depth and decoding speed, then distinguish workload categories such as code, prose, JSON and retrieval. He explicitly separates that inference from recovering actual prompts or answers: the attack observes timing, not their contents. Memory and compute isolation do not automatically eliminate signals from hardware operations that affect the whole GPU.

The walkthrough follows the trace from repeated memory reads to frequency analysis, token rates and layer signatures. Similar decoding speeds make tempo alone a weak fingerprint; the additional layer signal helps distinguish models with related architectures. Workload inference in the demonstrated setup depends on speculative decoding, whose acceptance patterns change step timing. Brzak then moves to a separate GPU on an NVSwitch connected H100 server and shows a weaker but still informative signal across NVLink. These are results from the tested configurations, rather than a claim that every shared deployment leaks equally. He closes with the operator choices that follow: consider tenant placement, understand the different isolation and communication tradeoffs, and observe the probing workload on the GPU itself.


Speaker info:
- https://www.linkedin.com/in/branislav-brzak/
- https://github.com/bane-stealthium

episodes.title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard
episodes.description:
An on call agent drops a billing database, restarts a production server and scales a service from four pods to 40, adding $420 an hour to the bill. Kim Maida's staged triage demo shows what happens when an agent receives standing API keys and an administrator's database credentials. Private data, untrusted tickets and access to external services combine into the lethal trifecta. The agent can do useful work, but its credentials give it far more authority than any one ticket requires. A human approval button alone cannot tell it which actions the user is actually authorized to approve.

Maida walks through delegated authorization using OAuth token exchange: carry the user's identity through the agent and MCP server, evaluate policy at a security token service and issue short lived credentials scoped to the requested access. She also explains Keycard's approach to intent based authorization, which she identifies as a proposal rather than a finalized standard. The second demo uses task based policy instead. Customer data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal is allowed, and a server restart stays blocked even after approval because the user's role cannot authorize it. Scaling proceeds when the user has the required authority. The demos make identity, delegation and policy decisions visible throughout the request chain, while keeping authorization distinct from whether an agent's answer is correct.

episodes.title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
episodes.description:
While one financial planner is on a client call, an agent drafts another client's cash flow or insurance analysis. The planner reviews every recommendation before anything reaches the client. At Range, Matthew Ragone and his colleagues built the skills behind that workflow without writing code. Six months in, he reports 24 skills across the company, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the same approach without a mandate. The change came from capturing how the firm actually works: what a planner checks first, which questions must be asked and where an agent must stop.

Ragone breaks the process into five steps: pick a repeated workflow whose output you can judge, teach it with real cases, package the judgment into a skill, test it five to ten times and ship it with an owner and a separate reviewer. Narrating why you open a document matters more than listing the clicks. Questions and limits belong in the skill alongside the procedure, including the rule that an agent drafts but never sends recommendations to a client. Testing exposes missing questions and confident mistakes; ownership keeps the instructions current as the firm's practices change. The remaining challenge is how to check quality at scale when the output requires professional judgment.

episodes.title: The Next Trillion Internet Users Still Don’t Have an Identity — Adi Singh, AgentMail
episodes.description:
Adi Singh let an agent run unsupervised to recruit other agents. It started calling itself a prophet of persistent identity.

NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT
Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes

Adi Singh, co-founder of AgentMail, argues that agent identity won't be issued by a new spec but accumulated on the surfaces humans already use, like email, the way MCP spread by bringing tools to apps people already lived in. He shares what happened when he let an agent run unsupervised to sign up other agents, explains why existing surfaces are both a trust surface and an attack surface, and walks through Telnyx's autonomous agent signup, where an AgentMail inbox lets an agent verify itself, get an API key and stay reachable for billing and support. He closes with what will break as agent numbers grow.

In this video:
- Why identity is accumulated, not issued
- How MCP spread by bringing tools to existing surfaces
- Trust vs attack surface: email's strengths and risks for agents
- A real autonomous agent signup flow with Telnyx

episodes.title: Decoupling the Brain from the Hands: Claude Managed Agents (Part 1 of 4) — Anthropic
episodes.description:
The first version of Claude Managed Agents put everything in one container. Here's why Anthropic split it apart.

NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT
Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes

Priyanka Phatak, who leads the Claude Managed Agents engineering team at Anthropic, defines an agent as a model in a loop with tools, plus a harness and a sandbox, and explains why harnesses encode assumptions that go stale with each new model. She walks through the first architecture, where the session, harness and sandbox shared one hard-to-debug 'pet' container, and the redesign into an append-only session log, a brain (harness plus Claude) and hands (sandboxes and tools). Credentials stay out of the sandbox and time to first token dropped about 90%. Then she introduces the core APIs with a simple joke-teller agent.

This is part 1 of 4 of the Claude Managed Agents workshop from Anthropic.

In this video:
• Why harnesses carry model-specific assumptions
• Decoupling session, harness and sandbox into replaceable parts
• Injecting credentials at an egress proxy so Claude never sees them
• The core flow: environment, agent, session, events
